articles.summary: By Tyler Thomas, Engineering Manager In commercial AI, eighteen months is an eternity. Microarchitectures turn over, memory bandwidth doubles, and rack-level thermal envelopes are rewritten before the thermal paste on last year’s deployment has even dried. In aerospace and defense, eighteen months may not get you through preliminary design reviews and initial environmental screening. This cadence mismatch is the central dilemma of modern tactical computing: Defense programs often run on 5- to 10-year lifecycles, but modern edge processing operates on an 18-month commercial silicon clock. If you design a mission system around a monolithic custom compute architecture, you are virtually guaranteed to field a legacy system. By the time an armored vehicle or an airborne ISR pod enters operational service, the deep neural networks it was intended to run have evolved past the compute capability of the silicon bolted inside it. Yet, simply buying commodity enterprise servers is typically a non-starter. A commercial datacenter box shaken on a tactical vehicle will shear connections, choke on dust, and succumb to dirty power transients within hours.
